title: Adolescent Depression and Suicide Prevention: Evidence-Based, Multi‑Tier Strategies
summary: Suicide remains a leading cause of adolescent mortality, tightly linked to depression. Effective prevention requires a layered approach across pediatric primary care, schools, families, and digital/acute care settings. Evidence supports universal screening, safety planning with lethal‑means counseling, brief contact interventions, CBT/IPT for depression, and stepped referral pathways. School-based social-emotional learning and nurse-led programs contribute to population-level risk reduction. Implementation quality and equitable access are decisive.
clinicalQuestion: Which strategies prevent suicidal ideation, attempts, and deaths among adolescents with or at risk for depression, and how should clinicians operationalize these strategies across care settings?

keyMoments.title: Primary care as prevention hub
keyMoments.body: Train clinicians to screen, assess acute risk, initiate safety plans, restrict lethal means, and provide warm handoffs to specialty care; emerging trials target low-cost scalable models in primary care [2], [3], [4].

keyMoments.title: Depression treatment reduces suicide risk
keyMoments.body: Treating adolescent depression with evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT/IPT) and, when indicated, medication with close monitoring can lower suicidal ideation/behaviors; vigilant observation is essential during the first 12 weeks and dose changes [5], [6].

keyMoments.title: School systems amplify reach
keyMoments.body: School-based social-emotional learning, trusted adult engagement, and nurse-led protocols improve protective factors and help-seeking; realist and integrative reviews support effectiveness when well-implemented [7], [8].

keyMoments.title: Rising post-pandemic urgency
keyMoments.body: Admissions for adolescent suicide attempts surged during COVID-19, highlighting the need for rapid access pathways and coordinated reentry after hospitalization [9].

sections.title: Multi‑Tier Prevention and Treatment Blueprint
sections.blurb: A practical sequence clinicians and school partners can implement to lower suicide risk linked to adolescent depression.

steps.title: Universal identification
steps.body: Implement validated, age-appropriate screening for depression and suicide risk in primary care and schools with clear escalation algorithms. Pediatric primary care training emphasizes screening, assessment, and intervention as standard functions [2].

steps.title: Risk stratification and immediate safety
steps.body: For positive screens, assess ideation, intent, plan, access to lethal means, prior attempts, and acute comorbidity. Create a collaborative written safety plan, restrict lethal means, and ensure same-day crisis linkage when indicated [2], [5].

steps.title: Initiate evidence-based depression care
steps.body: Start CBT or IPT; add antidepressants when indicated with shared decision-making and safety monitoring. Experts recommend close monitoring for suicidal thoughts/behaviors for at least 12 weeks and after dose changes [5], with depression a major suicide risk factor [6].

steps.title: Brief contact and follow-up
steps.body: Use proactive check-ins (calls/texts/portals) to reinforce safety plans and appointment adherence. Trials aim to operationalize low-cost scalable primary care follow-up models to reduce risk [3], [4].

steps.title: School partnership
steps.body: Coordinate with school nurses and counselors for reentry after crises and to embed social-emotional learning and trusted-adult engagement—approaches associated with improved protective factors and reduced risk behaviors [7], [8], [9].

steps.title: Address social determinants and equity
steps.body: Integrate family engagement, address bullying, and connect to community supports. Population data show suicide as a major mortality contributor, underscoring the need for equitable access across settings [1], [8], [9].

sections.title: What to Implement Now
sections.blurb: High-yield elements with strong face validity and implementation support.

cards.title: Primary care bundle
items: Train clinicians in suicide risk assessment, safety planning, and means restriction; standardize workflows [2].
Use validated screeners at defined intervals with EHR prompts and same-day risk pathways [2].
Establish warm handoffs to mental health and crisis services with rapid appointment access [2], [3].

cards.title: Treatment and monitoring
items: Offer CBT/IPT for depression; consider antidepressants when indicated with family education [5], [6].
Schedule close monitoring for at least 12 weeks after antidepressant initiation or dose changes [5].
Document and rehearse a personalized safety plan with warning signs, coping strategies, and contacts [5].

cards.title: School-based prevention
items: Embed social-emotional learning curricula that enhance coping and connectedness; meta-analytic support for SEL benefits [8].
Empower school nurses and trusted adults with protocols for identification, brief intervention, and referral [7], [8].
Coordinate post-hospitalization reentry plans to stabilize supports and monitor risk [9].

cards.title: Crisis response
items: Activate emergency evaluation for imminent risk (intent, plan, means) and consider hospitalization [5].
Ensure lethal means counseling and environmental safety before discharge; use caring contacts afterward [2], [5].
Provide family guidance on monitoring, medication storage, and follow-up adherence [5].
